primary_meaning: In mainstream Christian teaching, oil most commonly symbolizes the Holy Spirit, especially the Spirit's anointing, presence, and empowering. Anointing with oil marked prophets, priests, and kings as set apart and empowered by God, and this is read typologically as pointing to the Spirit's anointing of Christ (the 'Anointed One'/Messiah) and of believers.
primary_basis: 1 Samuel 16:13 (Samuel anoints David and the Spirit rushes upon him)
Exodus 30:22-33 (holy anointing oil for consecrating priests and the tabernacle)
Zechariah 4:1-6 (lampstand and olive oil linked to 'not by might... but by my Spirit')
Isaiah 61:1 / Luke 4:18 ('the Spirit of the Lord is upon me, because he has anointed me')
Acts 10:38 ('God anointed Jesus of Nazareth with the Holy Spirit and with power')
2 Corinthians 1:21-22 (God anointed us and gave the Spirit as a seal)
Psalm 23:5 ('you anoint my head with oil')
Matthew 25:1-13 (oil in the lamps of the wise virgins, often read as the Spirit or spiritual readiness)

alternatives.meaning: Healing and restoration: oil as a medicinal/ministerial sign used in prayer for the sick, foundational to practices of anointing the sick (and the Catholic/Orthodox sacrament of anointing).
basis: Luke 10:34 (the Samaritan pours oil and wine on wounds)

alternatives.meaning: Joy and gladness: oil as a festal symbol of blessing, celebration, and divine favor ('oil of gladness').
Consecration and setting apart for sacred office or use (priests, kings, prophets, sacred objects), emphasized as a distinct meaning rather than only a vehicle for the Spirit.
Blessing, abundance, and prosperity: oil as a staple of the land's fruitfulness and covenant blessing; also unity/fellowship in Psalm 133.

In the parable of the ten virgins specifically, oil read as faith, good works, grace, or spiritual preparedness rather than strictly the Holy Spirit (a long-standing exegetical divergence, e.g., Augustine and later commentators).
Light/illumination and witness: oil as fuel for lamps symbolizing testimony, devotion, or the word of God sustained in the believer.

notes: There is a broadly recognizable consensus that oil's chief symbolic referent is the Holy Spirit and His anointing, rooted in the Old Testament practice of anointing and the messianic title 'Anointed One.' However, oil is a multivalent biblical symbol, and interpreters routinely acknowledge secondary meanings (healing, joy, consecration, abundance) as context-dependent rather than competing. The most debated single text is Matthew 25 (the ten virgins), where commentators divide over whether the oil represents the Spirit, faith, works, or readiness. Sacramental traditions (Catholic, Orthodox) also institutionalize oil in chrismation/confirmation and anointing of the sick, reinforcing the Spirit-and-healing associations.
